title: REU Workshop
section: Welcome to an introductory R workshop for REU students
text:
Welcome to an introductory R workshop for REU students
This workshop is designed to serve as an introduction to R, data wrangling, and data visulatization. Since we only meet on a biweekly basis, it is adivsed that you continue to work on the skills on your own time.
In this document, I will share all of things we have dicussed and start to share new things. While the code in this document is not interactive, you can copy and paste it into your own script. In addition to this document, I will provide raw data scripts with minimal annotations, since the code will match what is shared here.
This course will be entirely focussed on R. While there is no required IDE, I encourage you to start with R studio.
Additionally, while Github fluency is not required, I will be sharing scripts and data via Github, so please create a username and send it to me via slack.

title: 1  What is code?
text: Start from the beginning

title: 1  What is code?
text:
What is programming?
Computer programming is the process of writing code to facilitate actions in a computer, application, or software program, and instructs them on how to perform.
Each ‘type’ of programming comes with it’s own language. A programming language is a vocabulary and set of grammatical rules for instructing a computer or computing device to perform specific tasks. Examples of programming languages include, but are not limited to , C, C++, Java, Python, and of course, R.
The purpose of programming is to find a sequence of instructions that will automate the performance of a task on a computer.

title: 2  What can R do?
text:
R as a calculator
First and foremost, R can act as calculator. This can be done in either the script or the console. Note that when you do any programming within the console, it does not automatically save as it does in the script.

2+2

[1] 4

2-2

[1] 0

(2+2)*2

[1] 8

(2+2)*2*2

[1] 16

(2+2)*(2*2)

[1] 16

title: 2  What can R do?
text:
How to annotate text
When wiritng code, it can be very helpful to leave yourself notes as to what you are doing, thinking, or to communicate with others who may encounter the same script. To accomplish this, we use the # [pound sign]. When you want comment something out, # must preceed the code. You can also annotate at the end of a line by following code with #.

#2+2
2+2 # this adds

[1] 4








Note



The annotation that follows the 2+2 code is not reported in the output becuase R is ignoring it.

title: 2  What can R do?
text:
Creating objects

How?
The first, and potentially most important, step with naming is which operator(s) to use when assigning names. There are two choices: = [equal sign] or <- [less than dash]. Generally, either of these will yield the same result for naming variables.

x = 1
y <- 2







Note



There are some operations that do not follow this rule. We will cover this more in the future as to when we can, and cannot, use either name-assigning operator.

title: 2  What can R do?
section: What can I use as a name?
text:
What can I use as a name?

Numbers
Number values, such as a year, cannot preceed a name. R will ackowledge this as code and it will report an error.

2026_name <- x

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:1:5: unexpected input
1: 2026_
        ^


However, numbers can follow text.

name_2026 <- x



Naming philosophy
As with anything, there are guidelines (which can be ignored) that encourage imformative naming. This will become especially important the further you get into data wrangling and data frame manipulation.

CamelCase
CamelCase, as you can see, follows the concept of combining upper- and lowercase letters to distinguish a name. For example, NewDataFrame is easier to read than newdataframe.

ThisNameIsNice <- thisnameisnotnice 



under_score
Another popular naming philosophy is the underscore. Rather than changing the case, you separate_words_with_an_underscore. Again, it goes without saying that this_is_easier_to_read than thisiseasiertoread.

coding_is_hard_enough <- letsnotmakeitharderthanithastobe




How informative should a name be?
When it comes down to it, that is up to the author. R studio (and most IDEs) do an excellent job auto-filling object names. There is something to be said about script cleanliness, but again, this is at the authors discretion. Persaonlly, I aire on the side of short, but imformative names.
For example:

new_data_2026 > new_data_frame_with_raw_data_2026
loc_x_subset.1 > subset_by_location_x_round_1







Note



As long as you do not start your object name with a number, naming comes at the discretion of the author. However, it is important to consider future use (by you and others).

title: 3  Types of objects
text: Types of objects

title: 3  Types of objects
text:
Numbers, characters, complex, oh my.

Types of data
In R, there are five types of data we may enctouner. Of these five, we commonly encounter two to three, depending on what you are doing. These include: numeric, character, logical, integer, and complex.

Numeric
Numeric is for, you guessed it, numbers. Within a data frame, numeric sometimes express as “double”, but are treated the same operationally.

# create a variable that is numeric  
x <- 10



[1] "numeric"








Note



In these code examples, the object type will print below the code. I have set it to do so using some hidden code. This will be consistent for the examples that follow below.
If you want to see that code, scroll to the title banner and select the </> Code link on the right side.




Character
If I wrap a number, word, or string of words with quotations, they are considered a character-type variable. When creating a character, you can use “quotation marks” or ‘apostrophes’.

# create characters using three examples 
x <- "character"
y <- '10'
z <- "all one object"



[1] "character"


[1] "character"


[1] "character"








Caution



If you attempt to combine a quotation mark with an apostrophe, your code will break. See the example below.



broken_name <- "x'

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:1:16: unexpected INCOMPLETE_STRING
1: broken_name <- "x'
2: 
                  ^




Logical
Logical operators comprise TRUE and FALSE statements.






Important



What happens when you do not use full caps for either true or false? Copy and paste the commented code into a script and see.



# assign logical values 
x <- TRUE 
y <- FALSE 
#x <- true
#class(true)



[1] "logical"


[1] "logical"




Integer
Integers are whole numbers without any fraction or decimal part. They are denoted in R by following a number with the uppercase letter “L”.

# assign an integer
x <- 10L



[1] "integer"




Complex numbers
Last, but not least, is the complex number. In our day-to-day wrangling and visualization, we seldom encounter this. However, it is important to know that complex numbers exist in R.

# i for imaginary 
x <- 10i



[1] "complex"

title: 4  Functionality with functions
section: Base R and some built in functions
text:
Base R and some built in functions
Functions are reusable blocks of code designed for a specific task, such as arithmetic. R comes with thousands of ready-to-use functions. Some of these include, mean, max, min, colnames, rm (remove), and the list goes on. When we want to use a function, we type the function name and add parentheses at the end, like so: mean(). The object we would like to manipulate with the funciton then goes inside the parentheses. Here is a link of base R functions.
For example:

x <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
mean(x)

[1] 3.5


For arithmetic functions, we can also add raw values.

mean(c(1,2,3,4,5,6))

[1] 3.5

title: 4  Functionality with functions
text:
Calling for help
Now, let’s say we would like to work with a function and do not know what it does or if it is the right choice for the task at hand. In R-studio, we can ask for help! If you preceed a function with a quesiton mark [?], a help sheet with code examples will be provided. Run the code below in your session and take a look!

?mean

title: 4  Functionality with functions
text:
Obtaining functions from packages
Ok great, we can calculate the mean and ask for help. But, what if base R does not have the function we want? You’re in luck!
There are many many more functions that can be called, but first we have to download the package where these functions reside. A package is exactly what it sounds like. They are boxes of functions, usually designed for specific tasks, that are free for all to download and use.
When we want to call in a package, we must first download it using the install.packages function. After this finishes downloading, we must then call the package into our working session using the library function.






Note



You only have to install a package once! But, every time you restart your R session, you must use the library function to call it into your working session.


Let’s download two packages: dplyr and ggplot2.
Run the code below in your session.

install.packages("dplyr")
install.packages("ggplot2")


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)







Note



Note that when using install.packages the package name must be in quotation marks, but when using library, it does not.

title: 5  Clean data with dplyr
text:
Time to start cleaning some data!
In this section, we will go over some important packages and key functions that will aid in R-based data wrangling. SO, without further ado, lettuce begin.

title: 5  Clean data with dplyr
text:
dplyr Examples
Let’s start by installing the needed packages.

install.packages("palmerpenguins")
install.packages("tidyverse")


library(tidyverse)

library(palmerpenguins)

The first thing I want to do is determine the names of all the columns within in this data set. I do this by using the base R function, colnames.

colnames(penguins) #the name of the clean data set

[1] "species"           "island"            "bill_length_mm"   
[4] "bill_depth_mm"     "flipper_length_mm" "body_mass_g"      
[7] "sex"               "year"             



select()
Let’s start by selecting for only the columns we are interested in. This can be useful when removing variables we are not currently working with.






Note



You do not have to save each change as a new object! The joy of dplyr is that you can manipulate your data frame as much as you want and not have to save it until you are ready. Additionally, you can save the changes as a new object which will maintain the integrity of the original if you must back track for whatever reason.


In this example, we use the select function to choose which columns we want to look at.

# select()
penguins %>% #pipe operator
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) # selecting columns species, bill_length, and      year 

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie            39.1  2007
 2 Adelie            39.5  2007
 3 Adelie            40.3  2007
 4 Adelie            NA    2007
 5 Adelie            36.7  2007
 6 Adelie            39.3  2007
 7 Adelie            38.9  2007
 8 Adelie            39.2  2007
 9 Adelie            34.1  2007
10 Adelie            42    2007
# ℹ 334 more rows


Using select again, what if I only want to remove one column? Instead of typing out every column we want, we can simple type out the one(s) we don’t.
In this example, I tell R to remove the sex column using the select function again.

# select()
penguins %>% #From the penguins data set
  select(-sex)# selecting all columns except for sex

# A tibble: 344 × 7
   species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
   <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
 1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
 2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
 3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
 4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA          NA
 5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
 6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
 7 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181        3625
 8 Adelie  Torgersen           39.2          19.6               195        4675
 9 Adelie  Torgersen           34.1          18.1               193        3475
10 Adelie  Torgersen           42            20.2               190        4250
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: year <int>


Within the select function, you can also look for items based on their spelling. This can be especially helpful if you suspect there to be a spelling error somewhere if your data set. In this example, we will search our data set for any variable name that starts with the letter ‘b’.

# select()
penguins %>% #From the penguins data set
  select(starts_with('b')) # selecting columns that start with 'b' and using starts_with

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm body_mass_g
            <dbl>         <dbl>       <int>
 1           39.1          18.7        3750
 2           39.5          17.4        3800
 3           40.3          18          3250
 4           NA            NA            NA
 5           36.7          19.3        3450
 6           39.3          20.6        3650
 7           38.9          17.8        3625
 8           39.2          19.6        4675
 9           34.1          18.1        3475
10           42            20.2        4250
# ℹ 334 more rows




rename()
What if I have a typo in a column name or really do not like what a column is called? Fortunately, renaming columns is easy. Notice with rename, there are two methods you can use. One without quotation marks, and one with. Regardless of which you use, the new name will always come first, followed by the old name.
In this example, using the rename function, I am changing ‘species’ to ‘Species and ’year’ to ‘Year’.

# rename()
penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% #selecting the columns I want to look at
  rename( #rename function. notice here the two methods of changing names
    Species = species, #changing species to Species without quotes
    "Year" = year #changing year to Year with quotes
  )

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   Species bill_length_mm  Year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie            39.1  2007
 2 Adelie            39.5  2007
 3 Adelie            40.3  2007
 4 Adelie            NA    2007
 5 Adelie            36.7  2007
 6 Adelie            39.3  2007
 7 Adelie            38.9  2007
 8 Adelie            39.2  2007
 9 Adelie            34.1  2007
10 Adelie            42    2007
# ℹ 334 more rows




arrange()
One of the first steps we take in Excel is sorting our data sets. The same is possible in R. We do this using the arrange function.
In this example, we will be sorting by bill length in an increasing order (smallest to largest). Notice here that R will default to the order of small-large with the arrange function.

# select() and arrange()
penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  arrange(bill_length_mm) #I want to look at bill length in an increasing order from      smallest to largest 

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie            32.1  2009
 2 Adelie            33.1  2008
 3 Adelie            33.5  2008
 4 Adelie            34    2008
 5 Adelie            34.1  2007
 6 Adelie            34.4  2007
 7 Adelie            34.5  2008
 8 Adelie            34.6  2007
 9 Adelie            34.6  2008
10 Adelie            35    2008
# ℹ 334 more rows


What if I want to look at bill length in decreasing order? We can accomplish this by nesting desc within the arrange function.

# select(), arrange(), and desc()
penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  arrange(desc(bill_length_mm)) #using the desc() function to command the order from      largest to smallest 

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species   bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>              <dbl> <int>
 1 Gentoo              59.6  2007
 2 Chinstrap           58    2007
 3 Gentoo              55.9  2009
 4 Chinstrap           55.8  2009
 5 Gentoo              55.1  2009
 6 Gentoo              54.3  2008
 7 Chinstrap           54.2  2008
 8 Chinstrap           53.5  2008
 9 Gentoo              53.4  2009
10 Chinstrap           52.8  2008
# ℹ 334 more rows


Now, let’s say we want to see bill length in the same descending order, but we want to order this by year. This is done with a very simple addition to our arrange() line. To accomplish this, we add the year variable first (remembering the the default for arrange is small-large) followed by the bill length command (which is the same as the previous example.)

# select() and arrange()
penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  arrange(year, desc(bill_length_mm)) #year and bill separated by a comma

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species   bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>              <dbl> <int>
 1 Gentoo              59.6  2007
 2 Chinstrap           58    2007
 3 Chinstrap           52.7  2007
 4 Chinstrap           52    2007
 5 Chinstrap           52    2007
 6 Chinstrap           51.7  2007
 7 Chinstrap           51.3  2007
 8 Chinstrap           51.3  2007
 9 Chinstrap           51.3  2007
10 Chinstrap           50.6  2007
# ℹ 334 more rows




filter()
We also have the ability to pull out rows with specific values. Let’s say I only want to look at data from 2007. To accomplish this, we will use the filter function.
In this example, we will be adding the filter function as well as recall our knowledge of operators within R.

# select() and filter()
penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, year) %>% 
  filter(year == 2007) #using the '==' operator to show everything with the year 2007

# A tibble: 110 × 4
   species bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl>         <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie            39.1          18.7  2007
 2 Adelie            39.5          17.4  2007
 3 Adelie            40.3          18    2007
 4 Adelie            NA            NA    2007
 5 Adelie            36.7          19.3  2007
 6 Adelie            39.3          20.6  2007
 7 Adelie            38.9          17.8  2007
 8 Adelie            39.2          19.6  2007
 9 Adelie            34.1          18.1  2007
10 Adelie            42            20.2  2007
# ℹ 100 more rows


What if I want to see which penguins have bill lengths that are higher than the average length, but only from 2007? This can be accomplished by, again, adding an operator, but also calling another function. We will command R further with mean function from base R. Notice I am separating each line in the filter function with a comma. This allows me to add multiple commands within the same function.

# select(), filter(), and mean()

penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  filter(
    year == 2007,#using the '==' operator to show everything with the year 2007
    bill_length_mm > mean(bill_length_mm), # using '>' to view every row where the bill length is greater than the avg bill length 
  ) 

# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: species <fct>, bill_length_mm <dbl>, year <int>








Warning



WAIT! This output is telling me that there are no instances of a bill length that are greater than the avarage from 2007… That seems impossible, no? So, what is the issue?
ALSO! There is no error message here. It is important to investigate the outputs we obtain because the code may run, but not be accomplishing what we think it is.


First, let’s look at the columns of interest again.

penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year)

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie            39.1  2007
 2 Adelie            39.5  2007
 3 Adelie            40.3  2007
 4 Adelie            NA    2007
 5 Adelie            36.7  2007
 6 Adelie            39.3  2007
 7 Adelie            38.9  2007
 8 Adelie            39.2  2007
 9 Adelie            34.1  2007
10 Adelie            42    2007
# ℹ 334 more rows


There is an NA! Arithmetic functions, like mean, will break when provided an NA value. In this case, the issue was easily spotted in the first 10 rows that R printed from the new data set. If we wanted to view more of the data set to spot the error, we can add print to our code.

penguins %>% 
    select(species, bill_depth_mm, year) %>% 
    print(n = 20) # print 20 lines 

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species bill_depth_mm  year
   <fct>           <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie           18.7  2007
 2 Adelie           17.4  2007
 3 Adelie           18    2007
 4 Adelie           NA    2007
 5 Adelie           19.3  2007
 6 Adelie           20.6  2007
 7 Adelie           17.8  2007
 8 Adelie           19.6  2007
 9 Adelie           18.1  2007
10 Adelie           20.2  2007
11 Adelie           17.1  2007
12 Adelie           17.3  2007
13 Adelie           17.6  2007
14 Adelie           21.2  2007
15 Adelie           21.1  2007
16 Adelie           17.8  2007
17 Adelie           19    2007
18 Adelie           20.7  2007
19 Adelie           18.4  2007
20 Adelie           21.5  2007
# ℹ 324 more rows


Ok great, what if my data set is too big to scroll through an find an NA value? An easy solution to do a quick filter of the NA values to determine if there are any present.
Using filter again, I will nest the is.na function with the variable I am interested in. If there is an NA in this column, R will print those values.

penguins %>% 
    select(species, bill_depth_mm, year) %>% 
    filter(is.na(bill_depth_mm))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  species bill_depth_mm  year
  <fct>           <dbl> <int>
1 Adelie             NA  2007
2 Gentoo             NA  2009


Lovely! We’ve spotted that NAs are present and the likely cause for the broken code. Let’s get rid of those NAs and obtain the mean. Similar to filter with is.na, we can nest a function with mean to remove NAs from the arithmetic. This function is na.omit.

penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  filter(
    year == 2007,
    bill_length_mm > mean(na.omit(bill_length_mm)) 
  ) 

# A tibble: 55 × 3
   species bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie            46    2007
 2 Adelie            44.1  2007
 3 Gentoo            46.1  2007
 4 Gentoo            50    2007
 5 Gentoo            48.7  2007
 6 Gentoo            50    2007
 7 Gentoo            47.6  2007
 8 Gentoo            46.5  2007
 9 Gentoo            45.4  2007
10 Gentoo            46.7  2007
# ℹ 45 more rows


We can also get rid of all of the NAs first by adding na.omit as the first function in our stream of code.

penguins %>% 
    na.omit()%>% 
    select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
    filter(
    year == 2007,
    bill_length_mm > mean(bill_length_mm)
  ) 

# A tibble: 54 × 3
   species bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Adelie            46    2007
 2 Adelie            44.1  2007
 3 Gentoo            46.1  2007
 4 Gentoo            50    2007
 5 Gentoo            48.7  2007
 6 Gentoo            50    2007
 7 Gentoo            47.6  2007
 8 Gentoo            46.5  2007
 9 Gentoo            45.4  2007
10 Gentoo            46.7  2007
# ℹ 44 more rows




count()
Let’s say we are interested in manipulating our data set by species.
I want to know how many species I have to further filter this set. To accomplish this, I will use the the count function to view how many species I have and their associated values within the data set.

# count()
penguins %>% 
  count(species)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species       n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie      152
2 Chinstrap    68
3 Gentoo      124


It appears there are three species within my data set. For one reason or another, I want to filter out Adelie from further interpretations. To do this, I will add another line below the bill length filter.
This new line says when species equals Chinstrap OR Gentoo, keep them in the data set.

# select() and filter()
penguins %>%
    na.omit() %>% 
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  filter(
    year == 2007,#using the '==' operator to show everything with the year 2007
    bill_length_mm > mean(bill_length_mm),# using '>' to view every row where the bill length is greater than the avg bill length
    species == "Chinstrap" | species == "Gentoo" # look in species and pull out chinstrap and gentoo. | allows to command two species, similar to 'or'
  ) 

# A tibble: 52 × 3
   species bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Gentoo            46.1  2007
 2 Gentoo            50    2007
 3 Gentoo            48.7  2007
 4 Gentoo            50    2007
 5 Gentoo            47.6  2007
 6 Gentoo            46.5  2007
 7 Gentoo            45.4  2007
 8 Gentoo            46.7  2007
 9 Gentoo            46.8  2007
10 Gentoo            49    2007
# ℹ 42 more rows


Another way to accomplish the same task is to tell R which values to exclude, rather than include. This is done by using the ‘does not equal’ operator to command R to return every species value that is not Adelie.

# select () and filter()
penguins %>%
    na.omit() %>% 
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  filter(
    year == 2007,#using the '==' operator to show everything with the year 2007
    bill_length_mm > mean(bill_length_mm),# using '>' to view every row where the bill length is greater than the avg bill length 
    species != "Adelie" #does not equal operator
  ) 

# A tibble: 52 × 3
   species bill_length_mm  year
   <fct>            <dbl> <int>
 1 Gentoo            46.1  2007
 2 Gentoo            50    2007
 3 Gentoo            48.7  2007
 4 Gentoo            50    2007
 5 Gentoo            47.6  2007
 6 Gentoo            46.5  2007
 7 Gentoo            45.4  2007
 8 Gentoo            46.7  2007
 9 Gentoo            46.8  2007
10 Gentoo            49    2007
# ℹ 42 more rows

#the output is the same!



mutate()
Now, let’s create some new columns and row values. With mutate I can add a new column with any information I would like.
Let’s start with a simple example of adding “new_column” with only the letter “x” in each row. Notice with these new columns, the first step is to name the new column and then command R what to put in.

penguins %>% 
    na.omit() %>% 
    select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
    mutate(new_column = "x")

# A tibble: 333 × 4
   species bill_length_mm  year new_column
   <fct>            <dbl> <int> <chr>     
 1 Adelie            39.1  2007 x         
 2 Adelie            39.5  2007 x         
 3 Adelie            40.3  2007 x         
 4 Adelie            36.7  2007 x         
 5 Adelie            39.3  2007 x         
 6 Adelie            38.9  2007 x         
 7 Adelie            39.2  2007 x         
 8 Adelie            41.1  2007 x         
 9 Adelie            38.6  2007 x         
10 Adelie            34.6  2007 x         
# ℹ 323 more rows


Ok, what about adding a new column that is based on a condition? For example, every time species “Adelie” is present I want an “x” and for the other species I want a “y”. I can do this using the case_when function which acts similar to an if/or statment.
To check that this works, I will follow mutate with group_by and slice_head. This will group the data frame by species and then allow me to take the first five values of each species change to check that my new column contains the correct information.

penguins %>% 
    na.omit() %>% 
    select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
    mutate(new_column = case_when(species == "Adelie" ~ "x", # if species is Adelie, add an x
    .default = "y")) %>% # if species is not Adelie, add a y
    group_by(species) %>% 
    slice_head(n = 5)

# A tibble: 15 × 4
# Groups:   species [3]
   species   bill_length_mm  year new_column
   <fct>              <dbl> <int> <chr>     
 1 Adelie              39.1  2007 x         
 2 Adelie              39.5  2007 x         
 3 Adelie              40.3  2007 x         
 4 Adelie              36.7  2007 x         
 5 Adelie              39.3  2007 x         
 6 Chinstrap           46.5  2007 y         
 7 Chinstrap           50    2007 y         
 8 Chinstrap           51.3  2007 y         
 9 Chinstrap           45.4  2007 y         
10 Chinstrap           52.7  2007 y         
11 Gentoo              46.1  2007 y         
12 Gentoo              50    2007 y         
13 Gentoo              48.7  2007 y         
14 Gentoo              50    2007 y         
15 Gentoo              47.6  2007 y         


Let’s say we want to add a new column combining species and year and a new column with the rounded values of bill length. We will be using the mutate function here. Along with this, we then want to rearrange our data set for viewing purposes of our new variables. This will be done with the select function.
In this example, I have created the column ‘sp_year’ which will contain both species and year, but keep their respective values separated by a dash. I then create a new column of the rounded bill length values using the round function. Lastly, using the select function, I command R to order this data set as follows.

# select(), mutate(), select()
penguins %>%
    na.omit() %>% 
  select(species, bill_length_mm, year) %>% 
  mutate(
    sp_year = paste(species, "-", year), #adding a new column named 'sp_year' and pasting the species column and year column with a dash between them. 
    rn_bill_length_mm = round(bill_length_mm) #creating a column of rounded bill lengths 
  ) %>% 
  select(species, year, sp_year, bill_length_mm, rn_bill_length_mm) #placing these new columns an order I would like 

# A tibble: 333 × 5
   species  year sp_year       bill_length_mm rn_bill_length_mm
   <fct>   <int> <chr>                  <dbl>             <dbl>
 1 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           39.1                39
 2 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           39.5                40
 3 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           40.3                40
 4 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           36.7                37
 5 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           39.3                39
 6 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           38.9                39
 7 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           39.2                39
 8 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           41.1                41
 9 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           38.6                39
10 Adelie   2007 Adelie - 2007           34.6                35
# ℹ 323 more rows




summarize()
Now that we are confident in our wrangling, we can investigate some summary statistics.
First, let’s look at the means and standard deviations of both bill length and depth. This will be done by name new columns and then using either the mean function or sd function to produce a desired output.

# summarize ()
penguins %>% 
    na.omit() %>% 
  summarize( #summarize to run summary stats 
  bill_length_mean = mean(bill_length_mm), #new column with mean value of bill length
  bill_length_sd = sd(bill_length_mm), #new column with standard deviation value of bill length
  bill_depth_mean = mean(bill_depth_mm), #new column with mean value of bill depth
  bill_depth_sd = sd(bill_depth_mm) #new column with standard deviation value of bill depth
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  bill_length_mean bill_length_sd bill_depth_mean bill_depth_sd
             <dbl>          <dbl>           <dbl>         <dbl>
1             44.0           5.47            17.2          1.97


The last output was informative, but lets look a little deeper. I now want to group these new values by species.
In this example, I am telling R to group_by species, and then provide me with the means and standard deviations of bill length and depth.

# group_by() and summarize()
penguins %>% 
    na.omit() %>% 
  group_by(species) %>% #grouping by one column, species 
  summarize( #summarize to run summary stats 
    bill_length_mean = mean(bill_length_mm), #new column with mean value of bill length
    bill_length_sd = sd(bill_length_mm), #new column with standard deviation value of bill length
    bill_depth_mean = mean(bill_depth_mm), #new column with mean value of bill depth
    bill_depth_sd = sd(bill_depth_mm) #new column with standard deviation value of bill depth
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  species   bill_length_mean bill_length_sd bill_depth_mean bill_depth_sd
  <fct>                <dbl>          <dbl>           <dbl>         <dbl>
1 Adelie                38.8           2.66            18.3         1.22 
2 Chinstrap             48.8           3.34            18.4         1.14 
3 Gentoo                47.6           3.11            15.0         0.986


Following the trend of the last example, let’s further group our data set. I want to now see these same values but by species AND year. Using the group_by function again, we can accomplish this.
In this example, the only change is I added ‘year’ into my group_by function.

# group_by() and summarize()
penguins %>% 
    na.omit() %>% 
  group_by(species, year) %>% #grouping by two columns, species and year 
  summarize( #summarize to run summary stats 
    bill_length_mean = mean(bill_length_mm), #new column with mean value of bill length
    bill_length_sd = sd(bill_length_mm), #new column with standard deviation value of bill length
    bill_depth_mean = mean(bill_depth_mm), #new column with mean value of bill depth
    bill_depth_sd = sd(bill_depth_mm) #new column with standard deviation value of bill depth
  )

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.

  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.

title: 5  Clean data with dplyr
text:
Practice on your own
Make five new changes to the penguins or penguins_raw data sets! These changes can include the functions covered above or functions within dplyr we did not look at here. These changes do not have to be logical or have any rationale, but you must be able to explain what you did.
